standards.title: Check the Swift toolchain first
standards.rule: Before writing Swift to these standards, check the project's toolchain: treat Swift 6.3 as the baseline, skip the async and @concurrent rules on Swift 6.1 or earlier, and do not write Swift 6.4 features (the Task cancellation shield SE-0504, mapKeyedValues, @available(anyAppleOS ...), @diagnose, weak let / ~Sendable, borrow/mutate accessors, UniqueArray/UniqueBox, Ref/MutableRef, the Continuation type) unless the project builds with 6.4, using the older form instead.
standards.why: The source's baseline is Swift 6.3 (the current release as of August 2026, when it was written): everything in it compiles on 6.3 unless marked, its concurrency guidance assumes the Swift 6.2 model, and the 6.4 proposals are safe to plan around and unsafe to write on a toolchain that does not have them.

sources.evidence: Toolchain baseline: Swift 6.3; §15: Rows marked ⚠ are Swift 6.4, which has not shipped ... prefer the older form if it targets 6.3 or earlier

standards.title: Simplest, most static thing first
standards.rule: Start with the simplest, most static, most single-threaded code that works and move down each default only with a reason you can state: data as struct/enum until you need identity, sharing or inheritance; abstraction as a concrete type until code repeats across types; polymorphism as some P until you need heterogeneous storage; execution on the main actor, synchronously, until profiling shows a hang; memory as Array/String until profiling shows the cost; a safe API until C interop or a measured hot path.
standards.why: Swift is a progressive-disclosure language: buy dynamism (concurrency, reference semantics, existentials, unsafe pointers) only where you can point at the reason; every other rule applies this one.

sources.evidence: The through-line: Swift is a progressive-disclosure language; Model this hierarchy of defaults

standards.title: Value types by default
standards.rule: Model data as struct or enum, and use class only for identity, shared mutable state, inheritance or resource lifetime.
standards.why: Value types are the default in Swift, not a special case: a window or a database connection has identity, a Point, a Drink or a Material does not.

values.class-only-for: identity, shared mutable state, inheritance, resource lifetime

sources.evidence: §1 Default to struct and enum. Use class only for identity, shared mutable state, inheritance, or resource lifetime

standards.title: Declare with let by default
standards.rule: Declare with let by default and use var only for values you mutate.
standards.why: It is the same discipline as some before any and value before reference: start narrow, widen with cause.

sources.evidence: §1 let by default; var only when you mutate

standards.title: No mutable references inside structs
standards.rule: Never leave a struct with a mutable reference-type stored property as is: keep the referenced type immutable, expose only computed properties that forward to it, or make it a private stored property behind copy-on-write.
standards.why: Such a struct is neither a value nor a reference: copies share the object and mutations leak across copies.

sources.evidence: §1 A struct with a mutable reference-type property is neither a value nor a reference

standards.title: Copy-on-write for out-of-line storage
standards.rule: When a struct needs out-of-line storage, is large with several reference-typed fields and copied a lot, or is too large for an any P's 3-word inline buffer, wrap a final class in it and check isKnownUniquelyReferenced(&storage) before mutating, copying first if the storage is not unique.
standards.why: Copy-on-write gives out-of-line storage and value semantics, exactly as Array, String and Dictionary work; a large struct with three reference-typed fields costs three retains per copy versus one for a class, and a value too large for an existential's inline buffer is heap-allocated per copy until indirect storage makes it fit again.

sources.evidence: §1 Copy-on-write is how you get out-of-line storage and value semantics; §9 Struct storage is inline; class storage is out-of-line; An any P existential has a 3-word inline buffer

standards.title: Make invalid states unrepresentable
standards.rule: Design models so illegal states cannot be spelled: one enum State instead of a pile of optional stored properties (isSharing, selectedRows, shareTarget), enums for closed sets, private setters with a validating mutating method, and a strongly typed UUID instead of a String.
standards.why: Invalid combinations become unrepresentable, and a state change becomes atomic instead of a sequence of property writes you can forget to finish.

values.identifier: a strongly typed UUID instead of a String

sources.evidence: §1 Enums are the tool for "a fixed set of things" and for mutually exclusive state; §8 Design the model so illegal states can't be spelled

standards.title: Compose values into values
standards.rule: Build structs from value-type stored properties so the whole type has value semantics.
standards.why: A struct whose stored properties are all value types has value semantics for free, which makes undo, diffing and state restoration a single code path instead of one per property.

sources.evidence: §1 Composing values yields a value

standards.title: Noncopyable types for unique ownership
standards.rule: Use a noncopyable type (~Copyable) for uniquely owned things such as a file descriptor, a bank transfer or an open resource, and mark its finishing method consuming.
standards.why: Suppressing the copy turns 'you must not run this twice' from an assertion into a compile error and makes deinit on a struct meaningful; consuming lets the compiler prove it is the last use.

sources.evidence: §1 Noncopyable types (~Copyable) express unique ownership

standards.title: Throw recoverable, trap on mistakes
standards.rule: Throw for recoverable errors and use precondition or fatalError for programmer mistakes.
standards.why: A failed network call keeps the program running; an out-of-bounds index means the code is wrong and must halt before the bug becomes a security issue.

sources.evidence: §2 Recoverable → throw. Programmer mistake → precondition/fatalError

standards.title: Errors carry their context
standards.rule: Make error types enums whose cases carry context as associated values (case duplicateFriend(String), not case duplicateFriend).
standards.why: The context is the whole point of the error.

sources.evidence: §2 Enums with associated values make the best error types

standards.title: guard for errors, if let to unwrap
standards.rule: Use guard for error conditions and if let for the ordinary unwrap.
standards.why: guard forces the exit path.

sources.evidence: §2 guard for error conditions, because it forces the exit path

standards.title: Typed throws only internally
standards.rule: Use typed throws (throws(MyError)) only for internal functions, error-forwarding generic code and constrained environments, and untyped throws for public API.
standards.why: Boxing any Error can be too costly in constrained environments, while untyped throws keeps your freedom to change a public error type later.

sources.evidence: §2 Typed throws (throws(MyError)) are for internal functions, error-forwarding generic code, and constrained environments

standards.title: Force-unwrap only with a stated invariant
standards.rule: Force-unwrap only where you can state the invariant, and prefer a failing #require or precondition with a message over a bare !.
standards.why: Swift error handling is about making the failure paths visible.

sources.evidence: §2 Errors and optionals: make the failure paths visible; Force-unwrap only where you can state the invariant

standards.title: Main actor first, then step down
standards.rule: Start every app entirely on the main thread and add concurrency only in this order, without skipping steps: async/await to hide latency (network, disk); @concurrent for your own expensive work only after Instruments (Time Profiler, hangs) shows a hang and the code cannot be made faster without concurrency; an actor only when too much main-actor state forces tasks to hop back constantly.
standards.why: Single-threaded code goes a long way and most apps never need to leave it; concurrency has real cost (task allocation, scheduling and reasoning), and this is where agents go wrong most often because the model changed in Swift 6.2.

sources.evidence: §3 Start every app entirely on the main thread; The progression, in order. Do not skip steps; Profile before you offload

standards.title: Enable Approachable Concurrency everywhere
standards.rule: Turn on the Approachable Concurrency build setting in every Swift project.
standards.why: It dramatically reduces the number of concurrency errors you will see.

sources.evidence: §3 Turn on the right build settings first. Enable Approachable Concurrency in every project; §16 both dramatically reduce the number of errors

standards.title: MainActor default isolation for app modules
standards.rule: Set Default Actor Isolation to MainActor for app and UI-facing modules (in a package: swiftSettings: [.defaultIsolation(MainActor.self)]).
standards.why: It is the default for new app projects in Xcode 26, and it deletes most of your @MainActor annotations.

sources.evidence: §3 For app modules and UI-facing modules, also set Default Actor Isolation to MainActor

conflicts: skills/opendesigner/scripts/engine.py export_swift: DesignTokens.swift carries no nonisolated marking, so turning Default Actor Isolation to MainActor in the app target that holds it (skills/opendesigner-export/SKILL.md: 'Add to the iOS target') makes every DS token main-actor isolated; checked with swiftc 6.4 (-swift-version 6 -default-isolation MainActor): a @concurrent function that reads DS.Motion.durationShort does not compile.

standards.title: Libraries ship nonisolated APIs
standards.rule: Never set main-actor-by-default on a general-purpose library; make its APIs nonisolated (nonisolated on a type covers all its members, Swift 6.1+) rather than @MainActor or @concurrent, so clients decide where work runs.
standards.why: nonisolated runs wherever it is called from, which makes it the right default for library APIs because the caller decides.

sources.evidence: §3 Do not set main-actor-by-default for a general-purpose library; nonisolated: this is the right default for library APIs; Quick Reference: A library API's isolation

conflicts: skills/opendesigner/scripts/engine.py export_swift writes build/swift/DesignTokens.swift with `public enum DS {}`, `public extension DS { enum Colors ... }` and `private func dsColor(...)` and no isolation annotation, and skills/opendesigner-export/SKILL.md says to add it to the iOS target; compiled there with Default Actor Isolation = MainActor (swiftc 6.4, -swift-version 6 -default-isolation MainActor), every token is main-actor isolated: reading DS.Motion.durationShort in a @concurrent function and DS.Radius.borderWidth4 in a nonisolated Shape.path(in:) are compile errors, while marking the enum, the extension and dsColor nonisolated compiles clean. standards.title: @concurrent moves heavy work off-main
standards.rule: Do not count on async to leave the current actor: when your own CPU-heavy work has to leave the main thread (after profiling, STD-swift-15), mark it @concurrent (@concurrent func … async), not Task.detached or DispatchQueue.global().
standards.why: In Swift 6.2 an async function runs where it was called from, while @concurrent always switches to the concurrent thread pool.

sources.evidence: §3 The rule that changed; Quick Reference: Move work off the main thread

review.message: On Swift 6.2 or later, move your own heavy work off the main thread with a @concurrent async function, not DispatchQueue.global().

standards.title: No tasks for trivial work
standards.rule: Do not spawn a task for trivial work such as reading a UserDefaults value.
standards.why: A child task for that costs more than it saves.

sources.evidence: §3 Don't spawn a task for trivial work

standards.title: One task per end-to-end operation
standards.rule: Put work that must happen in order in one task and give independent operations separate tasks.
standards.why: The runtime can then interleave the independent operations.

sources.evidence: §3 One task per end-to-end operation

standards.title: Nothing carried across an await
standards.rule: Re-check your assumptions after every await; never hold a lock or a blocking primitive (DispatchSemaphore, NSCondition) across one, and never rely on thread-local storage across one; restructure instead.
standards.why: await is a suspension point that breaks atomicity: state can change while you are suspended, and you may resume on a different thread.

sources.evidence: §3 await is a suspension point, and it breaks atomicity; Quick Reference: Blocking primitive across await

standards.title: Actor methods are transactions
standards.rule: Mutate actor state only in synchronous methods, keep async actor methods thin and consistent at every await, and after an await re-check state such as a cache (or dedupe the in-flight work) before writing it.
standards.why: Actors guarantee mutual exclusion, not transactions: between two awaits other work runs, so check cache, await download, write cache lets two tasks both miss, both download, and the second clobber the first.

sources.evidence: §3 Actor reentrancy: Mutate actor state in synchronous methods; Keep async actor methods thin; The classic bug

standards.title: Never use actors for ordering
standards.rule: When work must run in order, use a task or an AsyncStream, not an actor.
standards.why: Actors are not FIFO: they run highest-priority work first, precisely to avoid priority inversion.

sources.evidence: §3 Actors are not FIFO

standards.title: Isolate shared mutable state
standards.rule: Hold shared mutable state in an actor or a @MainActor class, not a class plus a lock you must remember.
standards.why: A class plus a lock is only safe while every caller remembers the lock; an actor or a @MainActor class isolates its state, which is also why both are implicitly Sendable.

values.not: class + a lock you must remember

sources.evidence: Quick Reference: Shared mutable state; §4 Actors and @MainActor classes are implicitly Sendable

standards.title: Write Sendable on public types
standards.rule: Write Sendable explicitly on every public type you mean clients to share across isolation domains.
standards.why: Public types never get inferred sendability: marking one Sendable is a promise to your clients, so Swift makes you write it.

sources.evidence: §4 Public types never get inferred sendability

standards.title: Model classes non-Sendable on purpose
standards.rule: Keep most model classes neither @MainActor nor Sendable (a shared model class is non-Sendable or @MainActor, never Sendable plus manual locking), and make one nonisolated rather than Sendable when it must leave the main actor.
standards.why: Staying non-Sendable on purpose prevents half the model being mutated on the main thread while the other half is mutated in the background.

sources.evidence: §4 Most model classes should be neither @MainActor nor Sendable; Quick Reference: A shared model class

standards.title: Stop touching what you send
standards.rule: When you send a non-Sendable object to another isolation domain, make every mutation before the hand-off and never touch it afterwards.
standards.why: Sending is allowed as long as the sender stops using it; touching it afterwards is the error.

sources.evidence: §4 You can still send a non-Sendable object between domains

standards.title: @Sendable only across domains
standards.rule: Mark a function type @Sendable only when it genuinely crosses isolation domains.
standards.why: Closures capture state too.

sources.evidence: §4 Closures capture state too. Only mark a function type @Sendable if it genuinely crosses domains

standards.title: Unchecked promises are a last resort
standards.rule: Use @unchecked Sendable only on types with real internal synchronization (a Mutex or a lock), and nonisolated(unsafe) on a global only as a last resort, never to silence a warning.
standards.why: Both are promises the compiler cannot check.

sources.evidence: §4 @unchecked Sendable is a promise the compiler can't check

standards.title: Fix data races by not sharing
standards.rule: Fix a data-race error by working down this list: stop sharing (move the object into a local so each concurrent job gets its own); make it a Sendable value type; isolate it to an actor (the main actor or your own); only then use Mutex/Atomic from the Synchronization module (stored in let properties) or @unchecked Sendable.
standards.why: Not sharing is the fix for the overwhelming majority of real errors.

values.4: Mutex / Atomic (in let properties) or @unchecked Sendable

sources.evidence: §4 When you hit a data-race error, work down this list; Quick Reference: Fixing a data race

standards.title: Globals: let before locks
standards.rule: Make a global or static variable safe in this order of preference: a let; @MainActor; a Mutex; nonisolated(unsafe).
standards.why: Global and static variables are the most common source of errors.

sources.evidence: §4 Global and static variables are the most common source of errors

standards.title: Bridge callback APIs to the main actor
standards.rule: Annotate delegate protocols you own with @MainActor; for ones you do not own, mark the method nonisolated and use MainActor.assumeIsolated { } (or @preconcurrency on the conformance), and use @preconcurrency import only to silence sendability warnings from a module that has not migrated yet.
standards.why: assumeIsolated asserts rather than hopping, so it traps loudly instead of racing silently; @preconcurrency import is temporary, and the warnings come back, correctly, once the module migrates.

sources.evidence: §4 Bridging old callback APIs

standards.title: Prefer structured tasks for children
standards.rule: Run concurrent children as structured tasks: async let for a fixed, statically known number, withTaskGroup for a dynamic number (iterating results as they land), and withDiscardingTaskGroup when children return nothing, not N unstructured Tasks or a withTaskGroup you never drain.
standards.why: Structured tasks cannot outlive their block, are awaited automatically, and inherit cancellation, priority and task-local values; withDiscardingTaskGroup frees each child's resources immediately and cancels siblings on the first error.

sources.evidence: §5 Always prefer structured tasks; Quick Reference: Fixed/Dynamic number of parallel jobs; Children that return nothing

standards.title: Task { } only when no scope fits
standards.rule: Open a Task { } only when the work's lifetime does not fit a scope (a delegate callback, a button tap, a view appearing), inside the synchronous callback rather than making the callback async, and manage its cancellation yourself.
standards.why: It inherits actor isolation and priority, but unstructured tasks give you none of the automatic cancellation, awaiting or scoping of structured ones.

sources.evidence: §5 Task { } only when the work's lifetime doesn't fit a scope; Quick Reference: Work tied to a UI event

standards.title: Almost never use Task.detached
standards.rule: Almost never use Task.detached; if you need a detached root, put a task group inside it rather than detaching repeatedly.
standards.why: It inherits nothing: not isolation, not priority, not task-locals.

sources.evidence: §5 Task.detached almost never

review.message: Task.detached inherits nothing: use a structured task, Task { } for UI-event work, or a @concurrent function to leave the main actor.

standards.title: Check cancellation before expensive work
standards.rule: Check Task.isCancelled or call try Task.checkCancellation() before starting expensive work, in synchronous helpers too.
standards.why: Cancellation is cooperative: cancelling sets a flag; it stops nothing.

sources.evidence: §5 Cancellation is cooperative

standards.title: Cancellation handlers need real locks
standards.rule: For suspended work such as an AsyncSequence's next(), use withTaskCancellationHandler and protect the state it touches with an atomic or a lock, not an actor.
standards.why: The handler runs immediately and concurrently with the body, and you cannot guarantee ordering on an actor.

sources.evidence: §5 For work that's suspended rather than running, use withTaskCancellationHandler

standards.title: Bound how many children run
standards.rule: Never fan out one child per item over an unbounded list: start N children, then add a new one each time one finishes.
standards.why: The source names one task per element, unbounded, as the form to avoid for a dynamic number of parallel jobs.

sources.evidence: §5 Bound your concurrency; Quick Reference: withTaskGroup (bounded), not one task per element, unbounded

standards.title: Pass context through @TaskLocal values
standards.rule: Propagate context such as a request ID or a trace span with optional @TaskLocal values instead of threading a parameter through every signature.
standards.why: Task-local values flow down the task tree, and making them optional gives unbound reads a sensible default.

sources.evidence: §5 Task-local values (@TaskLocal) propagate context

standards.title: Resume a continuation exactly once
standards.rule: When bridging callbacks with withCheckedContinuation or withCheckedThrowingContinuation, resume exactly once on every path, and for delegate APIs that fire later store the continuation and nil it out when you resume.
standards.why: Never resuming hangs the caller forever; resuming twice is a fatal error.

sources.evidence: §5 Bridging callbacks: resume exactly once on every path

standards.title: AsyncStream for callback APIs
standards.rule: Iterate async sequences with for await / for try await, and adapt handler- or delegate-based APIs with AsyncStream / AsyncThrowingStream: construct the source inside the closure, yield from the handler, and clean up in onTermination.
standards.why: This is the source's pattern for turning an existing handler- or delegate-based API into an AsyncSequence.

sources.evidence: §5 AsyncSequence: iterate with for await / for try await. Adapt ... with AsyncStream

standards.title: No @MainActor on SwiftUI views
standards.rule: Leave @MainActor off SwiftUI views and view models (you almost never need it), and delete the ones you have once main-actor-by-default is on.
standards.why: View is @MainActor-isolated, and so is everything it contains, including @State, so you almost never need it.

sources.evidence: §6 View is @MainActor-isolated

review.message: SwiftUI views are already @MainActor-isolated: delete the annotation.

standards.title: Copy values into @Sendable SwiftUI closures
standards.rule: When you hit an isolation error in code SwiftUI runs off the main thread (APIs whose signature says @Sendable: visualEffect, Shape.path(in:), Layout requirements, onGeometryChange), do not send self: copy the one value you need into the closure's capture list (for example [pulse]).
standards.why: SwiftUI deliberately runs this code off the main thread to keep frames cheap, and the @Sendable in the API's signature is the signal.

sources.evidence: §6 SwiftUI deliberately runs some of your code off the main thread ... don't send self, copy the one value you need

conflicts: skills/opendesigner/scripts/engine.py export_swift: with DesignTokens.swift in a MainActor-default app target, reading a DS token inside .visualEffect warns 'main actor-isolated static property ... can not be referenced from a Sendable closure' and inside a nonisolated Shape.path(in:) is an error (swiftc 6.4, -swift-version 6 -default-isolation MainActor), so every token read in these closures needs the capture-list copy.

standards.title: Start animations on the event's frame
standards.rule: Start an animation that answers a gesture or scroll event with a withAnimation state change inside SwiftUI's synchronous action callback, on the same frame as the event, and open a Task only for the long-running work that follows; never make the callback async.
standards.why: SwiftUI's action callbacks are synchronous on purpose: time-sensitive UI updates must happen on the same frame as the event.

values.animation-start: the withAnimation state change in the synchronous callback

sources.evidence: §6 SwiftUI's action callbacks are synchronous on purpose

standards.title: State on the UI/async seam
standards.rule: Put a piece of state on the seam between UI and async work: the view starts a task, the async layer makes a synchronous mutation when it finishes, and the UI reacts.
standards.why: It keeps view logic synchronous and makes the async logic testable without importing SwiftUI.

sources.evidence: §6 Put a piece of state on the seam between UI and async work

standards.title: Concrete types before protocols
standards.rule: Start with neither a class nor a protocol: write concrete types, and factor a shared capability into a protocol (then generic code against it) only once you notice repeated code across them.
standards.why: Swift is a progressive-disclosure language: abstraction is bought only with a reason you can point at, and repeated code across concrete types (overloads with near-identical bodies) is that reason.

sources.evidence: §7 Don't start with a class. Don't start with a protocol either

standards.title: No protocol without customization
standards.rule: When every conformance would share the same default implementation, write a constrained extension on an existing protocol instead of a new protocol.
standards.why: A protocol with no per-type customization is a wasted protocol, and elaborate hierarchies cost compile time and binary size and buy nothing.

sources.evidence: §7 A protocol with no per-type customization is a wasted protocol; Quick Reference: Shared behavior, no customization

standards.title: Prefer has-a over is-a
standards.rule: When only some of a protocol's operations make sense for your type, wrap it in a generic struct that exposes exactly the API you mean (GeometricVector<Storage: SIMD>, not GeometricVector: SIMD) instead of refining the protocol.
standards.why: Refining the protocol would expose operations that do not make sense for the type.

sources.evidence: §7 Prefer has-a to is-a

standards.title: Customization points are requirements
standards.rule: Make anything a conforming type should be able to customize a protocol requirement, not a method that exists only in an extension.
standards.why: A requirement is dynamically dispatched; an extension-only method is statically dispatched, so a conformer's version shadows rather than overrides it and code that only knows any P calls the extension's.

sources.evidence: §7 A protocol requirement is a customization point

standards.title: Composition over class inheritance
standards.rule: Compose small values instead of building class inheritance.
standards.why: Class inheritance is monolithic (one superclass), intrusive (you inherit stored properties and initializer complexity), and leaves unwritten contracts about what may be overridden and when to call super.

sources.evidence: §7 Composition over inheritance

standards.title: Treat forced downcasts as a smell
standards.rule: Treat every forced downcast (as!) as a code smell and look for the type relationship it stands in for.
standards.why: It usually means a type relationship was lost to a class hierarchy or an existential.

sources.evidence: §7 A forced downcast is a code smell

review.message: A forced downcast usually means a type relationship was lost to a class hierarchy or an existential; restore it.

standards.title: some P by default
standards.rule: Write some P by default and change to any P only when you need to store arbitrary types (a heterogeneous collection, an optional underlying type, or hiding the abstraction).
standards.why: some keeps every type relationship, including associated types, and lets the compiler specialize; any erases associated types to their upper bounds and is opaque to the optimizer.

sources.evidence: §7 some vs any: Write some P by default

standards.title: Open an existential through some P
standards.rule: To call a method that takes an associated type on an any P, pass the existential into a function taking some P.
standards.why: Erasure works in producing position but not in consuming position; the compiler unboxes the existential and the type is fixed again inside that scope.

sources.evidence: §7 You cannot call a method that takes an associated type on an any P

standards.title: Constrained opaque types, caller-facing associated types
standards.rule: Hide concrete types behind constrained opaque types and existentials (some Collection<Element>), and declare primary associated types on your own protocols (protocol Container<Item>) only for the type callers actually supply, not implementation details like Iterator.
standards.why: They hide a type such as LazyFilterSequence<[Animal]> while still exposing the element type.

sources.evidence: §7 Constrained existentials and opaque types

standards.title: Pin cross-protocol relationships with where
standards.rule: Pin relationships across protocols with same-type requirements in where clauses (where Self.CropType.FeedType == Self).
standards.why: Without them 'grow then harvest' does not typecheck, and wrong conformances compile.

sources.evidence: §7 Same-type requirements in where clauses

standards.title: Homogeneous collections before any P
standards.rule: Store a homogeneous [MyModel] unless you need heterogeneity, and then use [any P] rather than a class hierarchy.
standards.why: A homogeneous array is densely packed, passes type info once and is specializable; [any Model] is the flexible-but-opaque option to take when you need it.

sources.evidence: §9 Homogeneous [MyModel] beats [any Model]; Quick Reference: Heterogeneous collection

standards.title: Clarity at the point of use
standards.rule: Judge every API name and signature first by how clearly it reads at the call site.
standards.why: Clarity at the point of use is the goal that outranks every other one in API design.

sources.evidence: §8 API design: clarity at the point of use

standards.title: No type prefixes in Swift-only APIs
standards.rule: Leave type prefixes off Swift-only APIs (keep them only where an API mirrors an Objective-C one), and avoid very general names taken from specific frameworks.
standards.why: Modules disambiguate, and general names read badly out of context and force manual disambiguation.

sources.evidence: §8 No type prefixes in Swift-only APIs

standards.title: Drop the leading get
standards.rule: Drop a leading get from async alternatives and from anything that returns its result directly (persistentPosts, not getPersistentPosts).
standards.why: It serves clarity at the point of use, the goal that outranks every other in API design.

sources.evidence: §8 Drop leading get

review.message: Drop the leading get from a function that returns its result directly (persistentPosts, not getPersistentPosts); a get that fills an out-parameter or calls a completion handler is not covered.

standards.title: Explicit access control at boundaries
standards.rule: State access control (private, internal, package, public) explicitly at module boundaries.
standards.why: Access control is documentation, and being explicit at the boundary is what forces the sendability and API-evolution decisions.

sources.evidence: §8 Access control is documentation

standards.title: Know which of four costs you pay
standards.rule: Before optimizing, name which of the four low-level costs you are paying: function calls, memory layout, allocation or copies.
standards.why: Low-level Swift performance is dominated by these four costs; for allocation, global is free, stack is cheap (one subtraction) and heap is expensive (search plus locking).

values.costs: function calls, memory layout, allocation, copies

sources.evidence: §9 Low-level Swift performance is dominated by four costs. Know which one you're paying

standards.title: Do algorithmic work before micro-optimizing
standards.rule: Do the algorithmic work before any micro-optimization: every time you write a loop, try replacing it with a call to an algorithm.
standards.why: The largest wins are almost never micro-optimizations.

sources.evidence: §9 But do the algorithmic work first

standards.title: Know the complexity you call
standards.rule: Use removeAll(where:) instead of Array.remove(at:) in a loop, and popFirst() instead of re-slicing a Data per byte.
standards.why: remove(at:) in a loop is O(n²) against O(n) total, and per-byte re-slicing is O(n²) against O(1); both were 100×+ regressions hiding behind clean-looking code.

sources.evidence: §9 Know the complexity of what you call; Quick Reference: Removing matching elements

standards.title: Size hot pipelines once
standards.rule: In a per-pixel or per-element hot loop, size the output once and write into it instead of chaining map/flatMap/filter.
standards.why: Each chained stage allocates an array: elegant is not fast.

sources.evidence: §9 Chained map/flatMap/filter allocate an array per stage

standards.title: Profile a test in Instruments
standards.rule: Decide to optimize with Instruments' Time Profiler and Allocations run against a test (secondary-click the test's run button, then Profile), not intuition, and read the signals: platform_memmove is accidental copying, a million transient allocations are intermediate arrays, swift_beginAccess is runtime exclusivity checks, swift_retain/swift_release is reference-counting traffic.
standards.why: Profiling a test measures exactly the code you care about.

sources.evidence: §9 Then profile; Quick Reference: Deciding to optimize

standards.title: final and whole-module optimization
standards.rule: Mark classes you do not intend to subclass final and build with whole-module optimization.
standards.why: final turns dynamic dispatch static and unlocks inlining; whole-module optimization can prove it for you and enables generic specialization, which is where generics stop costing anything.

sources.evidence: §9 final on classes you don't intend to subclass

standards.title: Array until profiling says InlineArray
standards.rule: Keep Array and String for storage until profiling shows the cost, and only then use InlineArray<N, T> for fixed-size storage in a hot path, never for storage that gets copied or shared.
standards.why: InlineArray stores elements inline with no heap allocation, reference counting, or uniqueness or exclusivity checks, but it is the wrong choice if it gets copied or shared.

sources.evidence: Hierarchy of defaults: Memory row; §9 InlineArray<N, T> (Swift 6.2); Quick Reference: Fixed-size buffer in a hot path

standards.title: Span, not unsafe pointers
standards.rule: Reach contiguous storage through Span / RawSpan / OutputSpan (.span, .bytes) instead of withUnsafeBufferPointer or Unsafe*Pointer, and keep Unsafe* for C interop or a measured hot path.
standards.why: Since Swift 6.2 Span is a safe, non-escaping, equally fast way to reach contiguous storage: pointer performance with no lifetime bugs, and the retains/releases disappear.

values.unsafe-only-for: C interop or a measured hot path

sources.evidence: Hierarchy of defaults: Safety row; §9 Span / RawSpan / OutputSpan; §14 Prefer Span over Unsafe*Pointer; Quick Reference: Direct access to contiguous memory

review.message: Use .span / .bytes / OutputSpan for contiguous storage; keep unsafe pointers for C interop or a measured hot path.

standards.title: async only when something awaits
standards.rule: Do not make a function async if it has nothing to await.
standards.why: Async functions keep their state on a per-task slab allocator and split into partial functions at each suspension point, with slightly higher call overhead than sync functions.

sources.evidence: §9 Async functions ... another reason not to make something async that has nothing to await

standards.title: Batch hops to the main actor
standards.rule: Batch hops to and from the main actor by pushing the loop into functions that take arrays (loadArticles/updateUI) instead of hopping twice per iteration.
standards.why: Each hop to or from the main actor costs a real context switch.

sources.evidence: §9 Hops to and from the main actor cost a real context switch

standards.title: Never depend on deinit timing
standards.rule: Never write code that depends on when a deinit runs: keep deinit for verification, publish metrics or fire global effects from a defer at the call site, and use Xcode's Optimize Object Lifetimes build setting to surface these bugs.
standards.why: An object's guaranteed lifetime ends at its last use, not the closing brace; observed lifetimes come from the optimizer and will change, so effects in deinit are sequenced against optimizer decisions. Optimize Object Lifetimes shortens observed lifetimes toward the guaranteed minimum.

sources.evidence: §10 An object's guaranteed lifetime ends at its last use; Keep deinit side effects local; Optimize Object Lifetimes build setting ... will surface exactly these bugs

standards.title: weak and unowned only break cycles
standards.rule: Use weak or unowned only to break reference cycles, and never rely on reading a weak reference after its strong owner's last use; optional binding does not fix such a read, it is worse than a force-unwrap.
standards.why: Such a read may legitimately give nil, and optional binding there turns a loud crash into a silent wrong answer.

sources.evidence: §10 weak/unowned are for breaking reference cycles, nothing else

standards.title: Break cycles by restructuring
standards.rule: Break a reference cycle by not building it (factor the shared data into a third type both sides reference, turning the cycle into a tree), next by redesigning the API so the object is only reachable through a strong reference, and treat weak plus withExtendedLifetime as a patch, not a design.
standards.why: withExtendedLifetime works but shifts correctness onto you and spreads through a codebase.

sources.evidence: §10 Better than weak: don't build the cycle; Next best: redesign the API; Quick Reference: Breaking a reference cycle

standards.title: Swift Testing for new tests
standards.rule: Write new tests with Swift Testing (@Test and #expect), and keep XCTest only for UI automation (XCUIApplication), performance metrics (XCTMetric) and tests written in or catching Objective-C.
standards.why: XCTest remains required for exactly those three things.

values.xctest-only-for: UI automation (XCUIApplication), performance metrics (XCTMetric), tests that must be written in Objective-C or that catch Objective-C exceptions

sources.evidence: §11 Testing: Swift Testing by default; Quick Reference: A new test

standards.title: #expect with plain expressions
standards.rule: Write expectations as ordinary expressions with #expect (#expect(a == b)) instead of XCTAssertEqual-style functions.
standards.why: #expect captures and displays subexpression values on failure, with no family of assertion functions to memorize.

sources.evidence: §11 #expect(...) takes ordinary expressions

standards.title: try #require to stop a test
standards.rule: Use try #require(...) to stop a test on failure and to unwrap optionals, instead of continueAfterFailure = false.
standards.why: It lets you choose per expectation.

sources.evidence: §11 try #require(...); Quick Reference: Halting a test on failure

standards.title: Test suites are structs
standards.rule: Make test suites structs with setup in init, use a class or actor only when you need deinit for teardown, and nest suites to group them.
standards.why: A fresh instance is created per test function, so state cannot leak between tests.

sources.evidence: §11 Suites are structs

standards.title: Parameterize, don't loop or copy
standards.rule: Run the same test over many inputs with @Test(arguments: [...]) instead of copy-pasting or looping, using zip() for matched pairs rather than the full cross product.
standards.why: Each case runs independently, in parallel, individually re-runnable, with the failing argument named in the results.

sources.evidence: §11 Parameterize instead of copy-pasting or looping; Quick Reference: The same test over many inputs

standards.title: Traits carry test intent
standards.rule: Express test conditions and metadata with traits (.enabled(if:), .disabled("reason"), .bug(url), .tags(...), .timeLimit, and .serialized only when a test genuinely cannot run in parallel), and use @available rather than a runtime #available check.
standards.why: @available lets the testing library know about the condition, which a runtime #available check does not.

sources.evidence: §11 Traits carry intent

standards.title: Never comment a test out
standards.rule: Never comment a test out: use .disabled("reason") or .enabled(if:) for conditions, and wrap a test failing on something outside your control in withKnownIssue { } rather than .disabled.
standards.why: A disabled test still compiles, and withKnownIssue keeps it compiling and running and tells you when the issue is fixed.

sources.evidence: §11 never comment a test out; withKnownIssue { }; Quick Reference: A temporarily broken test

standards.title: confirmation for repeated callbacks
standards.rule: Test callbacks that fire N times with confirmation, and one-shot callbacks that have no async overload with withCheckedContinuation.
standards.why: These are the source's tools for testing callback-based code.

sources.evidence: §11 confirmation for callbacks that fire N times

standards.title: Keep tests parallel and random
standards.rule: Keep tests running in parallel and in randomized order, and refactor hidden inter-test dependencies instead of reaching for .serialized.
standards.why: Parallel, randomized runs are a feature: they surface hidden inter-test dependencies.

sources.evidence: §11 Tests run in parallel by default, in randomized order

standards.title: Migrate tests incrementally, strict interop
standards.rule: Migrate XCTest suites incrementally with both frameworks in one target, write new tests in Swift Testing today, and set test framework interoperability to complete or strict (not limited, never none).
standards.why: Those modes keep cross-framework issues as errors and point you at the Issue.record replacement.

sources.evidence: §11 Migrating: Test framework interoperability (swift-testing ST-0021; check your Xcode version for availability)

standards.title: Macros only for derivable code
standards.rule: Write a macro only when you are writing code the compiler could derive.
standards.why: The source reserves macros for boilerplate the compiler could have written, and only then.

sources.evidence: §12 Reach for a macro when you're writing code the compiler could derive, and only then

standards.title: Test macros as syntax transforms
standards.rule: Test macros as pure syntax-tree transforms with assertMacroExpansion, and learn a node's shape by setting a breakpoint in expansion and po-ing the syntax node.
standards.why: It is the fastest loop, and it is how you avoid bugs in code nobody reads.

sources.evidence: §12 Test macros as pure syntax-tree transforms with assertMacroExpansion

standards.title: Macros emit real diagnostics
standards.rule: When a macro does not apply, emit a real diagnostic (throw an error, or context.addDiagnostic for warnings and fix-its at a specific location), and never let it silently generate code that will not compile.
standards.why: The source gives no separate reason beyond the rule itself; the bullet before it sets the goal that misuse is a clean error at the call site, not a mess inside generated code.

sources.evidence: §12 Emit real diagnostics when the macro doesn't apply

standards.title: Log with Logger, not print
standards.rule: Log with Logger from os, one per subsystem and category, instead of print.
standards.why: Messages are stored in an optimized form and rendered only when displayed, so logging is cheap enough to leave in.

sources.evidence: §13 Logger from os, not print; Quick Reference: Diagnostics in shipping code

review.message: Use a Logger from os (one per subsystem and category) instead of print, debugPrint or NSLog.

standards.title: Opt log values into privacy
standards.rule: Mark a logged value privacy: .public only when it is genuinely not personal, and use .private(mask: .hash) to correlate values without exposing them.
standards.why: Non-numeric interpolations are redacted by default.

sources.evidence: §13 Non-numeric interpolations are redacted by default

standards.title: Log levels on purpose
standards.rule: Choose log levels deliberately, and log at error or fault for anything you will want in a bug report.
standards.why: Levels control persistence and cost, from debug (never persisted, fastest) through info and notice (the default) to error and fault (most persistent, slowest).

sources.evidence: §13 Levels control persistence and cost

standards.title: Log a correlation ID
standards.rule: Log a correlation ID (a task or request UUID) so a whole failure's history can be filtered from a device log archive (log collect --device --start ..., then filter by subsystem in Console).
standards.why: You can then diagnose a failure without reproducing it.

sources.evidence: §13 Log a correlation ID; Quick Reference: Logger + a correlation ID

standards.title: Keep unsafe regions tiny
standards.rule: When pointers are unavoidable, keep the unsafe region as small as possible, use buffer pointers (address plus count) rather than bare pointers, never let a pointer escape the closure that vends it, and run the Address Sanitizer.
standards.why: Unsafe means the API cannot fully validate its input, so violating its preconditions is undefined behavior, not a crash.

sources.evidence: §14 If you must use pointers

standards.title: Strict memory safety where it matters
standards.rule: Enable strict memory safety in security-critical modules.
standards.why: It forces every unsafe use to be acknowledged in source, which is what makes an audit possible.

sources.evidence: §14 Enable strict memory safety in security-critical modules

standards.title: Adopt Swift one file at a time
standards.rule: Adopt Swift into a C, Objective-C or C++ codebase one file at a time through interop instead of rewriting; to expose Swift functions back to C, use Swift 6.3's @c attribute (with @implementation when the declaration already exists in a header).
standards.why: Interop with C, Objective-C and C++ is bidirectional and incremental.

sources.evidence: §14 Interop is bidirectional and incremental ... Adopt Swift one file at a time; don't rewrite

standards.title: if and switch expressions
standards.rule: Initialize values with if/switch expressions instead of nested ternaries or an immediately-called closure (Swift 5.9+).
standards.why: Agents routinely write the older, longer form.

sources.evidence: §15 Modern syntax: Nested ternaries; an immediately-called closure to initialize a let

standards.title: Parameter packs over arity overloads
standards.rule: Use parameter packs (each T, and for over a pack) instead of overloads for 1, 2, 3… arguments (Swift 5.9+).
standards.why: Agents routinely write the older, longer form.

sources.evidence: §15 Modern syntax: Overloads for 1, 2, 3… arguments

standards.title: Use @Observable, not ObservableObject
standards.rule: Use @Observable instead of ObservableObject with @Published on every property (Swift 5.9+).
standards.why: Agents routinely write the older, longer form.

sources.evidence: §15 Modern syntax: ObservableObject + @Published on every property

standards.title: Observations instead of polling for changes
standards.rule: Watch an object with Observations { ... }, an AsyncSequence of transactional updates, instead of polling it for changes (Swift 6.2+).
standards.why: Agents routinely write the older, longer form.

sources.evidence: §15 Modern syntax: Polling an object for changes

standards.title: Concrete notification types over userInfo
standards.rule: Use concrete notification types (MainActorMessage / AsyncMessage) instead of NotificationCenter with stringly-typed userInfo (Swift 6.2+).
standards.why: Agents routinely write the older, longer form.

sources.evidence: §15 Modern syntax: NotificationCenter with stringly-typed userInfo

standards.title: Use Subprocess for scripting processes
standards.rule: Script with the Subprocess package (AsyncBufferSequence.strings() for line-by-line output) instead of Process plus pipes.
standards.why: Agents routinely write the older, longer form.

sources.evidence: §15 Modern syntax: Process + pipes for scripting

standards.title: Swift Regex over index math
standards.rule: Use Swift Regex (literals for brevity, RegexBuilder for structure) instead of hand-rolled string index math (Swift 5.7+).
standards.why: Agents routinely write the older, longer form.

sources.evidence: §15 Modern syntax: Hand-rolled string index math

standards.title: Swift Binary Parsing for binary formats
standards.rule: Parse binary formats with Swift Binary Parsing (ParserSpan, overflow-checked parsing initializers) instead of manual pointer parsing (Swift 6.2+).
standards.why: Agents routinely write the older, longer form.

sources.evidence: §15 Modern syntax: Manually parsing binary formats with pointers

standards.title: Foundation parsers inside regexes
standards.rule: Never hand-roll date or number parsing inside a regex; compose Swift Regex with Foundation's parsers (.date(...), .currency(...)).
standards.why: Swift Regex parsers compose with Foundation's real parsers.

sources.evidence: §15 Also worth knowing: never hand-roll date or number parsing inside a regex

standards.title: Explicit locale when parsing
standards.rule: Make the locale explicit when parsing rather than inheriting the system's.
standards.why: The source pairs it with composing Foundation's real parsers in Swift Regex.

sources.evidence: §15 Make the locale explicit rather than inheriting the system's

standards.title: Stop regexes backtracking across input
standards.rule: Use NegativeLookahead or Local (atomic groups) to stop a regex backtracking across a whole input.
standards.why: Without them a pattern can backtrack across the whole input.

sources.evidence: §15 use NegativeLookahead or Local (atomic groups)

standards.title: Migrate to Swift 6 target by target
standards.rule: Migrate to Swift 6 with Approachable Concurrency and (for app modules) main-actor-by-default turned on first, then per target in order: build with the new compiler in Swift 5 mode; enable complete concurrency checking, starting with the UI/app layer; fix warnings cheapest first; flip the target to the Swift 6 language mode; move to the next target.
standards.why: The order matters and mixing steps is how migrations stall; the UI/app layer is largely main-actor-annotated by the SDK so its fix rate is high, and the two settings dramatically reduce the number of errors.

values.1: build with the new compiler (Swift 5 mode)
values.2: enable complete concurrency checking, starting with the UI/app layer

sources.evidence: §16 Migrating an existing codebase to Swift 6; Enable Approachable Concurrency and ... main-actor-by-default before you start

standards.title: Refactor after migrating, separately
standards.rule: Never combine a significant refactor with enabling data-race safety; refactor afterwards, separately.
standards.why: Otherwise you will have to back out both.

sources.evidence: §16 Refactor afterwards, separately

standards.title: Module selectors when a type shadows a module
standards.rule: When a type shadows a module name, disambiguate with a module selector (Rocket::SaturnV) instead of Rocket.SaturnV (Swift 6.3+).
standards.why: Agents routinely write the older, longer form.

sources.evidence: §15 Modern syntax: Rocket.SaturnV when a type shadows a module → module selector Rocket::SaturnV (6.3)

standards.title: Raw identifiers for test names
standards.rule: Name tests with raw identifiers (@Test func `fruits have a tropical climate`()) instead of awkward camel-case function names.
standards.why: Agents routinely write the older, longer form.

values.since: Swift 6.2 (SE-0451); the source's table says 6.0, which is not when raw identifiers shipped [inferred from SE-0451 and the Swift 6.2 release]

sources.evidence: §15 Modern syntax: Awkward test function names → raw identifiers

standards.title: Inline and specialize only when measured
standards.rule: Reach for @inline(always) (paired with final on methods) and @specialized(where T == ...) (SE-0460) to pre-specialize a generic for hot concrete types only when you have measured the need.
standards.why: The source lists them as Swift 6.3 levers for a measured need, in line with measure first, then choose.

sources.evidence: §9 Shipped in Swift 6.3, when you've measured the need: @inline(always) ... and @specialized(where T == ...) (SE-0460)

standards.title: Exit tests for trap paths
standards.rule: Cover precondition and fatalError paths with exit tests (#expect(processExitsWith: .failure) { ... }), which run in an isolated child process on macOS, Linux, FreeBSD and Windows only.
standards.why: Exit tests run the trapping code in an isolated child process, so precondition and fatalError paths can be tested [inferred: a trap inside the test process would end the whole run].

sources.evidence: §11 Exit tests — #expect(processExitsWith: .failure) { ... } — cover precondition/fatalError paths in an isolated child process

standards.title: Format log values with format: and align:
standards.rule: Use format: and align: on logged values so logs are readable and column-selectable.
standards.why: They are free.

sources.evidence: §13 format: and align: are free — use them so logs are readable and column-selectable

standards.title: Property wrappers for access policies
standards.rule: Factor an access policy (@Argument, @Published, defensive copying, lazy, thread-local) into a property wrapper, and use result builders for declarative DSLs.
standards.why: The declaration site then states the policy in one word.

sources.evidence: §8 Property wrappers factor out an access policy ... so the declaration site states the policy in one word; Result builders for declarative DSLs
